title: Berberis nevinii

{{Short description|Species of shrub}} {{Speciesbox |image = Berberis nevinii 2.jpg |image2 = Berberis nevinii at Theodore Payne Foundation in La Tuna Canyon 01.jpg |status = G1 |status_system = TNC |status_ref = |status2 = LE |status2_system = ESA |status2_ref = |genus = Berberis |species = nevinii |authority = [[A.Gray]] | synonyms_ref = {{cite POWO |id=31495-2 |title=''Berberis nevinii'' A.Gray |access-date=13 December 2023}} | synonyms = {{Species list | Alloberberis nevinii | (A.Gray) C.C.Yu & K.F.Chung | Mahonia nevinii | (A.Gray) Fedde | Odostemon nevinii | (A.Gray) Abrams }} }} '''''Berberis nevinii''''' (syn. '''''Mahonia nevinii, Odostemon nevinii'''''{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OZYWAAAAYAAJ&q=abrams%20odostemon%20nevinii&pg=PA359|title=Contributions from the Department of Botany of Columbia University|date=1911|language=en}}), known by the common name '''Nevin's barberry''', is a species of flowering shrub in the [[Berberidaceae|barberry family]]. [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[southern California]], it is known from very few occurrences in the riparian areas of [[chaparral]] in inland canyons and foothills. It is a California state and United States federally listed [[endangered species]], since 1987https://nrm.dfg.ca.gov/FileHandler.ashx?DocumentID=109390&inline State of California, Natural Resources Agency, Department of Fish and Wildlife, Biogeographic Data Branch, California Natural Diversity Database (CNDDB) (2018). ''State and Federally Listed Endangered, Threatened, and rare plants of California.'' and 1998,U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (1998). ''Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Endangered or Threatened Status for Three Plants from the Chaparral and Scrub of Southwestern California'', Federal Register, vol. 63, no. 197, pp. 54956-54971.{{Cite web|url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=18826#null|title=ITIS Standard Report Page: Berberis nevinii|website=www.itis.gov|access-date=2019-02-02}} respectively. There are thought to be about 500 individuals remaining, with half of those being naturally occurring plants.{{Cite web|url=https://saveplants.org/national-collection/plant-search/plant-profile/|title=Plant Profile • Center for Plant Conservation|last=Heineman|first=Katherine|website=Center for Plant Conservation|language=en-US|access-date=2019-02-02}} It is also cultivated in gardens and parks as an ornamental and barrier plant.{{Cite web|url=https://www.laspilitas.com/nature-of-california/plants/422--mahonia-nevinii|title=Mahonia nevinii, Nevin's Barberry|last=Wilson|first=Bert|date=Apr 12, 2013|website=Las Pilitas Nursery|access-date=February 1, 2019}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.descansogardens.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Oak-Woodland-Plant-List.pdf|title=Oak Woodland Plant List|website=Descanso Gardens|access-date=Feb 1, 2019}} ==Description== ''Berberis nevinii'' is an erect, [[evergreen]], [[rhizomatous]] shrub approaching a maximum height of {{convert|4|m|ft}}. It has a dense foliage of dark green to bluish-green spiny-toothed, spear-shaped leaflets. It flowers in [[raceme]]s of 3 to 5 bright yellow cup-shaped, layered blossoms, that appear in spring between March and April.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jpw2AQAAMAAJ&q=nevin%20botanist%20barberry&pg=PA86|title=Tehachapi Renewable Transmission Project (TRTP): Environmental Impact Statement|date=2010|language=en}} The fruit is a spherical reddish [[Berry (botany)|berry]] appearing in bunches, in the summer, eventually darkening to a dark blue. == Taxonomy == === Taxonomic history === The plant was first described by American botanist [[Asa Gray]], in 1895, named in of honor fellow botanist, [[Reverend Joseph Cook Nevin]] (1835-1912), who was active in China and Southern California, particularly in the [[Channel Islands (California)|Channel Islands]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8ieqQs7hIREC&q=reverend%20joseph%20cook%20nevin&pg=PA842|title=CRC World Dictionary of Grasses: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology - 3 Volume Set|last=Quattrocchi|first=Umberto|date=2006-04-26|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781420003222|language=en}} It was later described in 1901 by [[Friedrich Karl Georg Fedde|Fedde]] and [[Franz Engel|Engel]] as ''Mahonia nevinii''.{{cite journal |last1=Abrams |first1=LeRoy |title=A Phytoseographic and Taxonomic Study of the Southern California Trees and Shrubs |journal=Bulletin of the New York Botanical Garden |date=1910 |volume=6 |issue=21 |pages=359–360 |url=https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.232443/page/359 |access-date=13 December 2023 |publisher=Lancaster Press |location=Lancaster, Pennsylvania}} Gray's original description for the plant was the following:
'''Berbericidae, [[Berberis]].''' '''B. Nevinii''', Gray, n. sp. Leaflets 3 to 7, [[Glossary of leaf morphology|oblong-lanceolate]], rather evenly and numerously [[Glossary of leaf morphology|spinulose-serrulate]], half to full inch long, obscurely reticulated; lowest pair toward base of petiole: [[raceme]] loosely 5-7-flowered, equalling [sic] or surpassing the leaves • pedicels slender. — S. California, near Los Angeles, ''Nevin''. Shrub 7 or 8 feet high, on a sandy plain. Berries juicy, ovoid, black or blue with a copious white bloom, called by Californian Mexicans ''Leña Amarilla'', and northward ''Oregon Grape'': leaflets ovate to oblong, usually 2 or 3 inches long: racemes commonly [[Fascicle (botany)|fascicled]] at summit of stem or in axils, subsessile, dense and numerously flowered; [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] rather short.{{Cite book|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/76504|title=Synoptical flora of North America.|last=Gray|first=Asa|date=1895–1897|publisher=American Book Company|volume=v.1 pt.1 (1895-1897)|location=New York}}
Following a reclassification in 1961, some botanists re-classified ''Berberis nevinii (see [[Berberis]])'' as ''Mahonia nevinii'' (see ''[[Mahonia]]),'' many commercial growers continue to use both names interchangeably.{{cite web |last1=Whittemore |first1=Alan T. |title=''Berberis nevinii'' - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Berberis_nevinii |website=Flora of North America |access-date=13 December 2023 |date=5 November 2020}}Loconte, H., & J. R. Estes. 1989. Phylogenetic systematics of Berberidaceae and Ranunculales (Magnoliidae). Systematic Botany 14:565-579.Marroquín, Jorge S., & Joseph E. Laferrière. 1997. Transfer of specific and infraspecific taxa from Mahonia to Berberis. Journal of the Arizona-Nevada Academy of Science 30(1):53-55.Laferrière, Joseph E. 1997. Transfer of specific and infraspecific taxa from Mahonia to Berberis. Bot. Zhurn. 82(9):96-99.{{Cite web|url=http://www.rareplants.cnps.org/detail/1056.html|title=CNPS Inventory Plant Detail|website=www.rareplants.cnps.org|access-date=2019-02-02}} As early as 1880, Gray stated that "[a]ll our species belong to the section ''Mahonia'', [[Thomas Nuttall|Nutt]]., which has evergreen unequally pinnate leaves, sessile spinulosely dentate leaflets, and dark blue globose berries."{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TK9LAQAAMAAJ&q=%22le%C3%B1a%20amarilla%22%20california&pg=PA14|title=Polypetalae, by W.H. Brewer and Sereno Watson. Gamopetalae, by Asa Gray. 2d (rev.) ed|last=California|first=Geological Survey of|date=1880|publisher=John Wilson and Son|language=en}} In a 1908 publication on fruits of California, [[Edward J. Wickson]], refers to other Californian barberries as belonging to the Mahonia genus and briefly describes ''[[Mahonia aquifolium|M. aquifolium]]'', ''[[Mahonia nervosa|M. nervosa]], and [[Mahonia pinnata|M. pinnata]]''{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OykSAQAAMAAJ&q=%22le%C3%B1a%20amarilla%22%20california&pg=PA38|title=California fruits and how to grow them|last=Wickson|first=Edward James|date=1909|publisher=Pacific Rural Press|language=en}}''.'' The latter is described as also being called ''leña amarilla'' (yellow firewood)'','' by Spanish Californians and noted for its "small, pleasant-flavored fruit". It also shares a name with ''Leña amarilla,'' a name given to [[Adesmia pinifolia]], a thorny shrub, native to the [[Andes]] of [[Mendoza Province|Mendoza]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TN1j9r4y1YsC&q=%22le%C3%B1a%20amarilla%22&pg=PA92|title=Catálogo de nombres vulgares de la flora argentina: (lista preliminar)|last=Peña|first=Martín Rodolfo de la|date=1997|publisher=Universidad Nac. del Litoral|isbn=9789875080096|language=es}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FTUFAAAAQAAJ&q=%22le%C3%B1a%20amarilla%22&pg=PA192|title=Botanical miscellany. Vol.1-3. [afterw.] The Journal of botany. pt.1, vol.2-4 [afterw.] The London journal of botany. Vol.1-7 [afterw.] Hooker's journal of botany and Kew garden miscellany. Vol.1-9. [Ed.] by W.J. Hooker|last=Hooker|first=sir William Jackson|date=1833|language=en}} The conflation of the common name in Spanish, may be due to the plant's rarity and ambiguity in classification during the early classification process. In his initial description of ''Mahonia'' species in California, Gray stated:
''B. Pinnata, [[Mahonia fascicularis]]'', DC. Hills about San Francisco Bay and southward to San Diego, thence East to New Mexico. Fruit pleasant to the taste and known to the Mexicans as ''Leña amarilla''. There has always been much confusion and is still some uncertainty respecting this species and its allies. [[Mariano Lagasca|Lagasca]]'s original description (published in 1803) professedly included specimens both from [[Monterey, California|Monterey]] and from [[Vancouver Island]], while the plant cultivated in the gardens from his seed, and figured under this name, appears to have been wholly the Oregon form, which [[Frederick Traugott Pursh|Pursh]] afterwards included with the low ''[[Berberis repens|B. repens]]'' in his description and figure of ''[[Mahonia aquifolium|B. Aquifolium]]''. [[Alexander von Humboldt|Humboldt]] and [[Aimé Bonpland|Bonpland]] afterward applied the name ''[[Berberis pinnata|B. pinnata]]'' to a Mexican plant, figured by them, and [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|DeCandolle]] at length included all, the Mexican, Californian, and Oregon together, under the name ''[[Mahonia fascicularis]]''. The question of synymy is most conveniently solved by retaining what has become the ordinary application of the names, ''[[Berberis fascicularis]]'' being limited to the Mexican species, which seems distinguishable from the Californian ''B. pinnata'' by its more numerous, more acuminate, and less shining leaflets.
Though debate between botanists on the correct classification continues in the 21st Century, as of 2023 the most common place ment of the species is again in ''Berberis'' as ''Berberis nevinii''.{{Cite WFO |title=''Berberis nevinii'' A.Gray |id=0000563588 |access-date=13 December 2023}} [[File:Berberis Nevinii Flowering in Spring.jpg|thumb|Berberis Nevinii in Spring Bloom]] [[File:Berberis Nevinii Fruit Berries.jpg|thumb|Berberis Nevinii Fruiting]] ==Distribution and habitat== Populations were historically found in washes of the [[San Fernando Valley]], near the [[Tujunga Wash|Tujunga wash]] (near the neighborhood of Garnsey).[http://www.theodorepayne.org/mediawiki/index.php?title=Berberis_nevinii California Natives Wiki: ''Berberis nevinii''] — [[Theodore Payne Foundation]] . accessed 7.8.2012. It was described in the 1910 [[New York Botanical Garden|Bulletin of the New York Botanical Garden]] as:
"A rare species apparently confined to the San Fernando Valley, where it occurs sparingly on the sandy slopes along the eastern edge of the valley. Upper Sonoran. Specimens examined: 'Los Angeles Valley,' probably San Fernando Valley, ''Nevin'', April, 1882; San Fernando, ''[[Francesco Franceschi (horticulturist)|Franceschi]]'', 1893; wash near Garnsey, San Fernando Valley, ''[[George Bird Grinnell|Grinnell]]'', Oct. 31, 1903"
The plant grows between 900 and 2,000 feet of altitude (300 – 610 m) in typical Southern California plant communities like [[coastal sage scrub]], chaparral, [[Cismontane chaparral|cismontane]] woodland, riparian scrub, sandy and gravelly places, and washes below 2150 feet. The plant is naturally occurring with [[Adenostoma fasciculatum|chamise]], [[Arctostaphylos|manzanitas]], California [[Salvia|sages]], [[ceanothus]] species, [[Dendromecon rigida|bush poppy]], and [[Peritoma arborea|bladderpod]].{{Cite web|url=https://calscape.org/Berberis-nevinii-(Nevin%27s-Barberry)|title=Nevin's Barberry, Berberis nevinii|website=calscape.org|access-date=2019-02-05}} There are currently about 21 known populations of the plant remaining, and almost all of them have fewer than 20 individuals, with some with as few as 5 individual plants.[http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=Mahonia+nevinii The Nature Conservancy] As of 1989, the USDA estimated that fewer than 500 plants exist in total. The populations are scattered throughout the [[San Gabriel Mountains]] and the [[Peninsular Ranges]] in [[Los Angeles County, California|Los Angeles]], [[San Bernardino County, California|San Bernardino]], and [[Riverside County, California|Riverside Counties]], its distribution possibly extending just into [[San Diego County, California|San Diego County]]. The USDA lists the plant as naturally occurring in [[Angeles National Forest]] and [[Cleveland National Forest]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/Rare_Plants/profiles/TEP/berberis_nevinii/index.shtml|title=Berberis nevinii, Nevin's barberry|website=www.fs.fed.us|access-date=2019-02-05}} Naturally occurring, extant populations can be found in Dripping Springs (near [[Aguanga, California|Aguanga]]), Scott Canyon, [[Agua Tibia Wilderness]], and a large population in [[Vail Lake]]/Oak Mountain Area. The populations in [[Devil's Gate Dam]], [[Arroyo Seco (Los Angeles County)|Arroyo Seco]], the [[Rose Bowl (stadium)|Rose Bowl]], [[Rimforest, California|Rimforest]], and [[San Timoteo Canyon|San Timoteo]] appear to be introduced, according to a 2009 [[Southern California Edison]] Environmental Report for a renewable [[transmission line]] project in the [[Tehachapi Mountains]]. The same report states that plants in the [[San Francisquito Canyon|San Francisquito canyon]] appear to be the only naturally regenerating population, despite having been introduced by seed. Threats to the species include habitat loss due to destruction, fragmentation of existing populations due to road-widening, degradation from urban development, off-road vehicle use, horseback riding, modified [[fire regime]]s, gold extraction activities, biocides, and displacement by [[introduced species|exotic plant species]], such as [[Spartium|Spanish broom]]. Additionally, it appears that the plant does not seed easily or frequently, which means that the community does not regenerate as quickly as competing species; the single individual at Dripping Springs successfully reproduced 56 years after it was initially documented. ==Cultivation== ''Berberis nevinii'' is cultivated as a [[Drought-tolerant plant|drought-tolerant]] [[ornamental plant]] by specialty [[plant nursery|plant nurseries]]. It is planted as a [[shrub]] in [[native plant]] and [[wildlife garden]]s, [[natural landscaping]] of parks in its range, [[xeriscaping|drought tolerant landscaping]], and for [[habitat]] [[Restoration ecology|restoration]] projects. It can serve as an impenetrable barrier [[hedge]], due to the spiny-toothed dense foliage. With berries appearing in the summer, earlier/later than other [[chaparral]] plants, it is an attractive bird food plant. The plant was introduced into cultivation in California by [[Theodore Payne]] in the 1920s.{{Cite web|title=Berberis nevinii, Nevin Barberry, Shrub, [Mahonia nevinii, Odostemon nevinii]|url=https://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=245|access-date=2019-02-02|website=San Marcos Growers}} ==See also== *[[California chaparral and woodlands]] *[[List of California native plants]] *[[Theodore Payne Foundation]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Berberis nevinii|Berberis nevinii—Mahonia nevinii}} *[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=15595 Jepson Manual eFlora (TJM2) treatment of ''Mahonia nevinii''] — ''formerly Mahonia nevinii''. *[http://calphotos.berkeley.edu/cgi/img_query?query_src=photos_index&where-taxon=Berberis+nevinii ''Berberis nevinii'' — U.C.
